questions.question: You have 3 pairs of trousers and 4 shirts. How many outfits (trousers + shirt)?
questions.explanation: Staged independent choices multiply: 3 × 4 = 12. (Adding, 3 + 4 = 7, is the common mistake.)

questions.question: How many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded among 8 runners?
How many different 3-person committees can be formed from 10 people?
questions.explanation: Order doesn't matter, so use C(10, 3) = 10! ÷ (3! × 7!) = 120. (720 would count each committee 6 times, once for every ordering of its three members.)

questions.question: Which situation calls for a COMBINATION rather than a permutation?
questions.explanation: In the lottery only *which* numbers you pick matters, not the order, so it is a combination. The other three all distinguish order or roles.

questions.question: There are C(49, 6) = 13,983,816 lottery tickets and exactly one wins. What is the chance that a single ticket wins?
questions.explanation: P = 1 ÷ 13,983,816, about 1 in 14 million. Counting the total number of outcomes is what makes the probability computable.
